name: Airy Isostasy Root
description: Computes the depth of the crustal root beneath topography under Airy isostasy, where mountains are supported by buoyant crustal material extending into the denser mantle. The root depth equals the crustal density times height, divided by the density contrast between mantle and crust.
notes: Densities must share the same unit and rhom must exceed rhoc for a positive root. This assumes local (Airy) compensation with a constant-density crust of uniform composition.

name: Pratt Isostasy Density
description: Computes the column density under Pratt isostasy, where topography is compensated by lateral density variations above a common depth of compensation. Higher topography h corresponds to a lower density rho0·D/(D+h) so that all columns exert equal pressure at depth D.
notes: D and h use the same length unit; taller columns must be less dense. Contrasts with Airy isostasy, which instead varies crustal thickness at constant density.

name: Geothermal Gradient Temperature
description: Computes the temperature at depth z by adding the geothermal gradient G times depth to the surface temperature T0. It assumes temperature rises linearly with depth.
notes: G is in °C per metre, so with a typical 25 °C/km use 0.025; z is in metres. The linear model ignores variations in thermal conductivity and heat sources.

name: International Gravity Formula (1980)
description: Computes normal (theoretical) gravity at sea level as a function of latitude using the 1980 International Gravity Formula. It captures how gravity increases from about 9.780 m/s² at the equator to roughly 9.832 m/s² at the poles due to Earth's rotation and flattening.
notes: Latitude phi must be in radians. This gives the reference ellipsoid gravity at sea level, excluding elevation and terrain (free-air and Bouguer) corrections.

name: Free-Air Gravity Correction
description: Computes the free-air correction applied to gravity measurements to account for the decrease of gravity with elevation above the reference ellipsoid. It adds 0.3086 mGal for each metre of elevation h.
notes: h is in metres and the result is in milligals (mGal). This corrects only for height in free air; it does not account for the mass of rock below the station (Bouguer correction).

name: Bouguer Slab Correction
description: Computes the Bouguer slab correction, which accounts for the gravitational attraction of the rock mass between the measurement station and the reference level, modeled as an infinite horizontal slab. It equals 0.04193 mGal per unit density and metre of thickness.
notes: Density rho must be in g/cm³ and thickness h in metres to yield milligals with this coefficient. It is subtracted from the free-air anomaly; terrain corrections are separate.

name: P-Wave Velocity
description: Computes the velocity of compressional (P) seismic waves in an elastic medium from its bulk modulus K, shear modulus mu, and density rho. It equals the square root of (K + 4/3·mu) divided by density.
notes: All inputs in SI units (Pa and kg/m³) give velocity in m/s. P-waves are always faster than S-waves in the same medium because of the added bulk-modulus term.

name: S-Wave Velocity
description: Computes the velocity of shear (S) seismic waves in an elastic medium as the square root of the shear modulus mu divided by density rho. Because fluids have zero shear modulus, S-waves cannot travel through them.
notes: Inputs in SI units (Pa and kg/m³) give velocity in m/s. S-waves are always slower than P-waves in the same solid material.

name: Poisson's Ratio (from Vp/Vs)
description: Computes Poisson's ratio of an elastic medium from its P-wave and S-wave velocities. The dimensionless ratio characterizes how much the material contracts laterally when stretched and depends only on the Vp/Vs ratio.
notes: Vp and Vs must share the same unit; the result is dimensionless. Poisson's ratio typically lies between 0 and 0.5 for common rocks, with 0.5 indicating a fluid-like medium.

name: Radiometric Age (Isochron)
description: Computes the radiometric age of a sample from the ratio of accumulated daughter isotope D to remaining parent isotope P, using the radioactive decay law. The age equals ln(1 + D/P) divided by the decay constant lambda.
notes: D and P share the same unit so their ratio is dimensionless; lambda is in 1/yr, giving age in years. Assumes a closed system with no initial daughter isotope.

name: Geomagnetic Dipole Field
description: Computes the total magnetic field strength of a geocentric dipole at radius r and magnetic latitude lat. The field falls off as 1/r³ and varies with latitude through the factor sqrt(1 + 3·sin²(lat)), being twice as strong at the poles as at the equator.
notes: Use SI units with r in metres and lat in radians; result is in tesla. This idealizes Earth's field as a pure centered dipole, ignoring higher-order and crustal components.

name: Curie Depth
description: Computes the Curie depth, the depth at which rock reaches the Curie temperature and loses its ferromagnetism, using a linear geothermal gradient. It divides the temperature rise from surface T0 to Curie point Tc by the gradient G.
notes: Tc and T0 are in °C and G in °C per metre, so use 0.025 for 25 °C/km; result is in metres. Assumes a constant gradient with no heat-production variation.

name: Gravity at Depth (uniform Earth)
description: Computes gravity at depth z inside an Earth of uniform density, where gravity decreases linearly from the surface value g0 to zero at the center. It multiplies g0 by (R − z)/R.
notes: R and z use the same length unit and z must not exceed R. The linear decrease holds only for a hypothetical uniform-density sphere; the real Earth's gravity actually rises slightly before falling.

name: Flexural Rigidity
description: Computes the flexural rigidity of an elastic plate, a measure of its resistance to bending, from Young's modulus Em, elastic thickness Te, and Poisson's ratio nu. Rigidity scales with the cube of thickness, so it is very sensitive to Te.
notes: Use SI units (Em in Pa, Te in m) to get rigidity in N·m; nu is dimensionless. The strong Te³ dependence means small thickness errors greatly affect the result.

name: Flexural Parameter
description: Computes the flexural parameter, the characteristic horizontal length scale over which an elastic lithospheric plate bends under a load. It is the fourth root of 4 times flexural rigidity Dr divided by the product of density contrast drho and gravity.
notes: Use SI units so the result is in metres; drho is the density difference between the material filling the flexure and that displaced beneath. Larger rigidity gives a broader, gentler deflection.

name: Postglacial Rebound Relaxation
description: Computes the remaining vertical displacement during postglacial rebound as the initial displacement u0 decays exponentially over time. After each relaxation time trel the displacement falls to about 37% (1/e) of its value.
notes: t and trel must use the same time unit; the result shares the length unit of u0. This single-exponential model idealizes the mantle as a single-viscosity Maxwell material.

name: Acoustic Impedance
description: Computes the acoustic (seismic) impedance of a material as the product of its density rho and wave velocity V. Impedance governs how much seismic energy is reflected at boundaries between layers.
notes: Use SI units (kg/m³ and m/s) to get impedance in kg/(m²·s). Contrasts in impedance between adjacent layers, not their absolute values, control seismic reflection strength.

name: Reflection Coefficient (normal incidence)
description: Computes the seismic reflection coefficient at normal incidence from the acoustic impedances of two layers as (Z2 − Z1)/(Z2 + Z1). It gives the fraction of wave amplitude reflected at the interface.
notes: Z1 and Z2 must share the same unit; the dimensionless result ranges from −1 to 1, where a negative value indicates a polarity reversal (reflection off a lower-impedance layer).

name: Critical Angle (Refraction)
description: Computes the critical angle of incidence at which a seismic wave passing from a slower layer (velocity V1) into a faster layer (V2) refracts along the interface. It equals the arcsine of V1/V2.
notes: Requires V2 greater than V1 so that V1/V2 is below 1; the result is in radians. Beyond this angle the wave is totally internally reflected and head waves form.

name: Earth Mass from Surface Gravity
description: Computes the mass of the Earth (or any planet) from its surface gravity g and radius R by inverting Newton's law of gravitation: mass equals g·R² divided by the gravitational constant G. It treats the body as a sphere.
notes: Use SI units (m/s², m) to get mass in kilograms. Assumes a spherically symmetric body; g here is the true gravitational acceleration, excluding rotation effects.

name: Adiabatic Temperature Gradient
description: Computes the adiabatic temperature gradient inside a convecting body, the rate at which temperature changes with depth when material moves without exchanging heat. It equals the thermal expansion coefficient alpha times gravity times temperature, divided by specific heat cp.
notes: Use SI units with T in kelvin; the result is in K/m and represents the background gradient in vigorously convecting regions such as the mantle or a stellar interior.

name: Thermal Diffusion Length
description: Computes the thermal diffusion length, the characteristic distance heat conducts in a given time t through a material of thermal diffusivity kappa. It equals the square root of kappa times t.
notes: Use SI units (m²/s and s) to get length in metres. It is an order-of-magnitude scale for how far a thermal signal penetrates, not a sharp boundary.

name: Geomagnetic Inclination
description: Computes the geomagnetic inclination, the angle at which the magnetic field dips below horizontal, from the geomagnetic latitude using the dipole relation tan(I) = 2·tan(latitude). The field is horizontal at the magnetic equator and vertical at the poles.
notes: Latitude is in radians and the result is inclination in radians. Valid for a geocentric axial dipole field, ignoring non-dipole and local anomalies.

name: Seismic Attenuation (Q)
description: Computes the amplitude of a seismic wave after traveling a distance x through a medium with quality factor Q, accounting for anelastic energy loss. The initial amplitude A0 decays exponentially, faster at higher frequency f and lower Q.
notes: Use SI units (x in m, V in m/s, f in Hz); Q and the amplitude ratio are dimensionless. Lower Q means stronger attenuation, so high frequencies are lost fastest with distance.

name: Gravitational Binding Energy (uniform sphere)
description: Computes the gravitational binding energy of a uniform-density sphere, the energy needed to disperse its mass to infinity against self-gravity. It equals 3·G·M² divided by 5·R.
notes: Use SI units (kg, m) to get energy in joules. Assumes constant density; a centrally condensed body like a real planet or star has larger binding energy for the same mass and radius.

name: Shear Modulus from S-wave Velocity
description: Computes the shear (rigidity) modulus of a rock or material from its bulk density and shear (S-wave) seismic velocity, mu = rho*Vs^2. It measures resistance to shape-distorting shear stress.
notes: Density and velocity must be in SI units (kg/m^3 and m/s) so the result comes out in pascals. Assumes an isotropic, elastic medium, as is standard in seismic velocity analysis.

name: Terrestrial Heat Flow (Fourier's Law)
description: Computes conductive terrestrial heat flow via Fourier's law, q = k·(dT/dz), combining rock thermal conductivity with the geothermal gradient (temperature rise per kilometre of depth).
notes: With conductivity in W/(m·K) and gradient in K/km, the product gives heat flow directly in mW/m^2, matching typical continental values of 40-90 mW/m^2. Assumes purely conductive, steady-state heat transport with no fluid advection.

name: Bulk Modulus from Vp, Vs, Density
description: Computes the bulk modulus of a material from density and its P-wave and S-wave seismic velocities, K = rho*(Vp^2 - (4/3)*Vs^2). It gives resistance to uniform (volumetric) compression.
notes: Density and both velocities must be in SI units for a result in pascals. Assumes an isotropic elastic medium; Vp must sufficiently exceed Vs for a physically meaningful positive bulk modulus.
